problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1

China's large scientific facility, the Spallation Neutron Source, was completed and put into operation in 2018; it has wide applications in many fields. Historically, Chadwick first confirmed the existence of the neutron in 1932 and measured its mass; in 1939 Hahn and co-workers discovered that bombarding uranium nuclei with neutrons can make them split, at the same time releasing neutrons and triggering a chain reaction. In order for the chain reaction to proceed in a sustained and controllable way, the neutrons released by the uranium nuclei can be slowed down (moderated) by elastic collisions. Relativistic effects are not to be considered.

(1) Chadwick bombarded stationary target nuclei of mass $m_1$ (hydrogen nuclei H or nitrogen nuclei $^{14}\mathrm{N}$, of mass $m_{\mathrm{H}}$ or $14m_{\mathrm{H}}$) with neutrons (of mass $m$) and observed their motion. Let the angle between the outgoing momentum of the target nucleus and the initial momentum of the incident neutron be $\alpha$. Derive the relations of the outgoing speed $v_1$ of the target nucleus and of the final speed $v$ of the neutron, respectively, to the initial speed $v_0$ of the neutron. In this experiment the maximum outgoing speed of the hydrogen nuclei was measured to be $3.30\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and the maximum outgoing speed of the nitrogen nuclei $4.70\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Find the values of $m$ and $v_0$.

(2) In the above experiment a nitrogen nucleus may also be struck successively by a beam of neutrons. Suppose the nitrogen nucleus is initially at rest, every neutron colliding with it has speed $v_0$, and every collision gives the largest possible increase of the speed of the nitrogen nucleus. Calculate after how many collisions the kinetic energy of the nitrogen nucleus is approximately equal to the initial kinetic energy of a neutron.

(3) Suppose the neutrons slowed down by many collisions are in thermal equilibrium, their speeds obeying the Maxwell distribution

$$f(v)=4\pi\left(\frac{m}{2\pi k_{\mathrm{B}}T}\right)^{3/2}v^{2}\,\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{mv^{2}}{2k_{\mathrm{B}}T}},$$

where $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ is the Boltzmann constant and $T$ is the absolute temperature of the system. Calculate, at thermal equilibrium, the kinetic energy corresponding to the most probable speed of the neutrons, and the most probable kinetic energy.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2

When two conducting spheres in an electric field come close to each other, the electric field between the conducting spheres is markedly enhanced. This problem explores this phenomenon. The vacuum permittivity $\varepsilon_0$ is known.

(1) The centre of an isolated conducting sphere of radius $R_0$ is at distance $a$ ($a>R_0$) from a stationary point charge $Q$. Find the magnitude of the image charge and its position.

(2) The conducting sphere is placed in a uniform external electric field of magnitude $E_0$; this external field can be regarded as produced, at the midpoint of the line joining them, by two equal and opposite point charges $\pm Q$ very far apart. Prove that the action of the induced charge of the conducting sphere is equivalent to an electric dipole formed by two image charges, and find the relation between the dipole moment of this electric dipole and the external field $E_0$.

(3) Outside the conducting sphere, two equal and opposite point charges $\pm q$ are separated by $\Delta l$; the electric dipole $q\Delta\boldsymbol{l}$ they form is placed radially near the conducting sphere of radius $R_0$, with the centre of the dipole at distance $r$ ($r\gg\Delta l$) from the centre of the conducting sphere. Find the magnitude of the image dipole moment of this dipole in the conducting sphere.

(4) In a uniform external electric field of magnitude $E_0$, two conducting spheres of radius $R_0$ are placed along the direction of the external field, their centres a distance $r$ ($r>2R_0$) apart. Find the distribution of the electric potential at any point $\mathrm{P}'(x,y)$ outside the conducting spheres in the plane through the two centres, and the distribution of the field strength along the direction of the line joining the two centres (recurrence relations may be used). Take the midpoint of the line joining the two centres as the origin of coordinates and the direction of this line as the $X$ axis.

(5) Prove that, if breakdown discharge is not considered, when the above two conductors are slowly brought infinitely close to each other, the electric field at the midpoint of the line joining the centres of the two spheres tends to infinity because of electrostatic induction.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3

A quantum heat engine is a heat engine that runs a cycle with quantum matter as the working substance. Below, a two-level atomic system is taken as an example to describe the working principle of a quantum heat engine. The average energy of a two-level atom is defined as

$$\langle E\rangle=p_0\cdot E_0+p_1\cdot E_1,$$

where $E_0$, $p_0$ and $E_1$, $p_1$ denote the energies and probabilities of the atom being in the ground state and in the excited state, respectively. For simplicity, assume $E_0=0$; during the cycle the energy difference between the excited state and the ground state is an adjustable parameter. The probability that the atom is in a state of energy $E$ obeys the Boltzmann distribution

$$p\propto\mathrm{e}^{-E/(k_{\mathrm{B}}T)},$$

where $T$ is the thermodynamic temperature and $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ is the Boltzmann constant. In a quasi-static process the change of the average energy is

$$\mathrm{d}\langle E\rangle=p_1\,\mathrm{d}E_1+E_1\,\mathrm{d}p_1,$$

where $p_1\,\mathrm{d}E_1$ is the energy change caused by the change of the energy level, corresponding to the work $\text{đ}W$ done by the surroundings on the two-level atomic system, and $E_1\,\mathrm{d}p_1$ is the energy change caused by the change of the probability, corresponding to the heat $\text{đ}Q$ transferred by the surroundings to the two-level atomic system.

(1) The two-level atomic system is put in contact with a heat reservoir of temperature $T$. Find the probability $p_0$ that the two-level atomic system is in the ground state and the probability $p_1$ that it is in the excited state at thermal equilibrium.

(2) The $P$-$V$ diagram of the classical Otto cycle is shown in Figure 2a, where A→B and C→D are isochoric processes and B→C and D→A are adiabatic processes. Sketch the relation between the energy difference $E_1$ of the two levels and the excited-state probability $p_1$ during the quantum Otto cycle, and calculate the heat transferred, the increase of internal energy and the work done on the surroundings in each of the four processes of the quantum Otto cycle.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2020-1-3-fig1.png

Figure 2a [绝热 = adiabatic]

(3) Similarly, calculate the heat transferred, the increase of internal energy and the work done on the surroundings in each process of the quantum Carnot cycle. Assuming that the temperature $T_h$ of the hot reservoir and the temperature $T_l$ of the cold reservoir in the quantum Carnot cycle are equal, respectively, to the highest and the lowest temperature of the quantum Otto cycle, compare the efficiencies of the quantum Otto engine and the quantum Carnot engine.

Problem 4

Since Yeh and Cummins observed in 1964 the Doppler frequency shift of light scattered by particles in flowing water, laser Doppler velocimetry has found wide application. To obtain sufficient scattered light intensity, tracer scattering particles of suitable size and concentration are usually seeded in the fluid; when laser light illuminates a moving particle it is scattered, and the velocity information of the particle (and of the fluid) is thereby obtained. Let the angle between the particle velocity $\boldsymbol{v}$ and the vertical be $\beta$.

(1) As shown in Figure 4a, a beam of light of frequency $f$ is scattered by a moving particle in the fluid. The propagation speed of light in the fluid is $c/n$ ($n$ is the refractive index of the fluid), and the particle moves with velocity $\boldsymbol{v}$ ($v\ll c/n$). The angles between the propagation directions of the incident light and of the observed scattered light and the particle velocity are $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$, respectively. Find the relation between the frequency shift $\Delta f$ of the scattered light relative to the incident light and the direction of the scattered light. Taking the particle speed $v=1\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and the light frequency $f=10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}$, can $\Delta f$ be detected directly with a spectrometer of resolution $5\,\mathrm{MHz}$?

The phases of the scattered light of the two beams on reaching the photodetector are $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$, respectively; the electric field vectors of the scattered light have approximately the same direction and both have amplitude $E_0$. The current output by the photodetector is proportional to the light intensity it receives, with proportionality constant $k$. Assuming that the frequency response range of the photodetector is $10^{2}\sim10^{7}\,\mathrm{Hz}$, find the expression for the output current of the photodetector. problems.title: Problem 5
problems.problem:
Problem 5

Interstellar medium exists in the vast cosmic space between the stars. Under the action of cosmic rays, molecules of the interstellar medium lose some of their electrons and become positive ions, while the electrons wander free, forming a plasma state. A pulsar is a rapidly rotating neutron star with an extremely strong magnetic field; the electromagnetic radiation from it observed on the Earth is a pulsed signal. Pulsar signals can be used for interstellar navigation and high-precision timekeeping; for this it is necessary to obtain the precise times of arrival of the pulses at the Earth, and to study the phase changes and dispersion of their electromagnetic radiation.

The distance from a pulsar to the Earth is $d$, and the mean number density of electrons in the interstellar medium is $n_{\mathrm{e}}$ (of the order of $10^{4}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$). Assume that there is a uniform static magnetic field $B$ in the medium (of the order of $10^{-10}\,\mathrm{T}$), directed parallel to the propagation direction of the electromagnetic waves. The electron mass $m_{\mathrm{e}}$, the electron charge $-e$ ($e>0$), the vacuum permittivity $\varepsilon_0$ and the speed of light in vacuum $c$ are known.

(1) Take the direction of the electromagnetic radiation from the pulsar to the Earth as the positive $z$ direction. For an electromagnetic wave of frequency $f$ the electric field is $E_x=E_0\cos(kz-2\pi ft)$, $E_y=E_0\cos\left(kz-2\pi ft\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, where $E_0$ and $k$ are the amplitude and the wave number of the electromagnetic wave, respectively. For simplicity, take $E_0$ to be constant and neglect the action of the magnetic field of the electromagnetic wave itself on the electrons. Find the gyration radius $R_{\mathrm{e}}$ of the electron motion.

(2) When a pulsar signal propagates in the interstellar medium, dispersion occurs; its propagation speed (the magnitude $v_{\mathrm{g}}$ of the group velocity) depends on the rate of change of the frequency of the electromagnetic wave with respect to the wave number: $v_{\mathrm{g}}=2\pi\dfrac{\mathrm{d}f}{\mathrm{d}k}$. Find the lowest frequency $f_{\mathrm{c}}$ of the electromagnetic waves of the pulsar signal that can pass through the medium and reach the Earth.

(3) Assuming that the mean electron number density $n_{\mathrm{e}}$ of the interstellar medium stays constant along the propagation path of the pulsar signal, by how much is the time of arrival at the Earth of the electromagnetic wave of frequency $f$ in the pulsar signal delayed compared with its propagation time in vacuum?

(4) It is observed that the electromagnetic waves of frequency $f$ that leave the pulsar simultaneously show a phase difference on arrival at the Earth. Find this phase difference (the approximations $\dfrac{e}{2\pi}\sqrt{\dfrac{n_{\mathrm{e}}}{\varepsilon_0m_{\mathrm{e}}}}\ll f$, $\dfrac{eB}{2\pi m_{\mathrm{e}}}\ll f$ may be used).

(5) If over an interval of length $a$ along the propagation path the electron number density shows a fluctuation $\Delta n_{\mathrm{e}}$, find the phase shift, caused by the fluctuation of the electron number density, of the electromagnetic wave of frequency $f$ in the pulsar signal after it passes through this interval.

problems.title: Problem 6
problems.problem:
Problem 6

Antiparticles were first predicted by Dirac's theory. In 1932, while studying cosmic rays, Anderson discovered the antiparticle of the electron, the positron. Since then, further antiparticles such as the antiproton have been discovered one after another.

Antiprotons can be produced by bombarding a stationary proton target with a beam of high-energy protons of energy $6.8\,\mathrm{GeV}$ per particle; the reaction is

$$\mathrm{p}+\mathrm{p}\to\mathrm{p}+\mathrm{p}+\underbrace{\mathrm{p}+\bar{\mathrm{p}}}_{\hookrightarrow\ \pi^{-}+\cdots}$$

When protons and antiprotons annihilate, $\pi^{-}$ mesons can be produced, so the antiproton beam is also accompanied by a large number of $\pi^{-}$ mesons. Figure 6a is a schematic diagram of the experimental set-up for detecting antiprotons. The stream of antiprotons $\bar{\mathrm{p}}$ and $\pi^{-}$ mesons passes successively through the scintillation counters $\mathrm{S}_1$, $\mathrm{S}_2$ and $\mathrm{S}_3$; $\mathrm{S}_1$ and $\mathrm{S}_2$ are a distance $l=12\,\mathrm{m}$ apart, and the Cherenkov counters $\mathrm{C}_1$ and $\mathrm{C}_2$ are placed between $\mathrm{S}_2$ and $\mathrm{S}_3$. A Cherenkov counter determines the speed of a charged particle by detecting Cherenkov radiation (the electromagnetic radiation excited when a charged particle moves in a medium faster than the speed of light in the medium). $\mathrm{C}_1$ records only the faster $\pi^{-}$ mesons, and $\mathrm{C}_2$ records only the slower antiprotons. In the experiment, the role of $\mathrm{S}_3$ is to check whether the preceding counting results are genuine.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2020-1-6-fig1.png

Figure 6a

(1) In the above reaction, assuming that the protons and the antiproton in the final state have approximately equal velocities, find the time $t_{\bar{\mathrm{p}}}$ the antiproton needs to travel from $\mathrm{S}_1$ to $\mathrm{S}_2$. If a $\pi^{-}$ meson has the same kinetic energy as the antiproton, find the time $t_{\pi^{-}}$ the $\pi^{-}$ meson needs to travel from $\mathrm{S}_1$ to $\mathrm{S}_2$.

(2) A charged particle moving with speed $v$ ($v>c/n$) passes through a medium of refractive index $n$. Find the angle $\theta$ between the propagation direction of the Cherenkov radiation produced and the direction of motion of the charged particle.

(3) A differential Cherenkov counter can record the number of particles with speeds in a certain interval. Figure 6b is the schematic cross-section of such a counter, which is rotationally symmetric about its axis (the dashed line in the figure). The light collection system consists of a spherical mirror of radius $R$ and an annular diaphragm of adjustable radius. When the angle $\theta$ between the propagation direction of the Cherenkov radiation and the direction of motion of the charged particle is very small, the spherical mirror focuses the Cherenkov radiation excited by the charged particle onto its focal plane, forming a ring of radiation of radius $r$, which is projected onto the counters. For the radiation excited by a charged particle of speed $v$, find the radius of the ring of light.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2020-1-6-fig2.png

Figure 6b [光环半径 = radius of the ring of light; 计数器 = counter; 环状光阑 = annular diaphragm; 球面镜 = spherical mirror; 粒子束 = particle beam]

(4) When an antiproton meets a proton, the annihilation reaction $\mathrm{p}+\bar{\mathrm{p}}\to3\pi^{0}$ occurs. The difference between the total kinetic energy of the particles in the final state of the reaction and the total kinetic energy of the particles in the initial state is the reaction energy $Q$. For simplicity, assume that the kinetic energies of the proton and the antiproton are negligible. The total kinetic energy of the three $\pi^{0}$ mesons in the final state is a constant, and the distribution of the total kinetic energy among the three $\pi^{0}$ mesons can be represented by a Dalitz plot. As shown in Figure 6c, the Dalitz plot is an equilateral triangle of height 1, and the distances from a point P to the three sides equal the fractions of the reaction energy carried as kinetic energy by the three $\pi^{0}$ mesons, i.e. $d_i=E_{k,i}/Q$, where $E_{k,i}$ is the kinetic energy of the $i$-th $\pi^{0}$ meson, $i=1,2,3$. Set up a coordinate system with the base as the $X$ axis, the midpoint of the base as the origin and the perpendicular bisector of the base as the $Y$ axis. Find the expression for the boundary of the region in which the point P may lie, in terms of the reaction energy $Q$, the $\pi^{0}$ meson mass $m_{\pi^{0}}$ and the speed of light in vacuum $c$. Also discuss the expression for the boundary of the region of the point P if $m_{\pi^{0}}=0$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2020-1-6-fig3.png

Figure 6c

Given: the speed of light in vacuum $c=2.998\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, the proton mass $M_{\mathrm{p}}=938.2720\,\mathrm{MeV}/c^{2}$, the neutral $\pi$ meson mass $m_{\pi^{0}}=134.9766\,\mathrm{MeV}/c^{2}$, the charged $\pi^{\pm}$ meson mass $m_{\pi^{\pm}}=139.5702\,\mathrm{MeV}/c^{2}$.

problems.title: Problem 7
problems.problem:
Problem 7

According to the chapter "Youzuo" of the Xunzi (《荀子·宥坐篇》), Confucius visited the ancestral temple of Duke Huan of Lu, where there was a qi (欹, qī) vessel, a "tilting vessel". Of the tilting vessel it is said: "When empty it tilts, when moderately filled it stands upright, when full it overturns." A real suspended tilting vessel is shown in Figure 7a: when the vessel is empty, its body is tilted; when moderately filled with water, its body stands upright; when filled with too much water, its body overturns. Figure 7b is the front cross-sectional view of the suspended tilting vessel. The outer contour of the whole vessel is a surface of revolution about the $Z$ axis; the $Z'$ axis is the symmetry axis of the bored inner cavity. The radii of the hemispherical shells of the inner wall and of the outer wall of the vessel are $R_1=R$ and $R_2=\sqrt{3}R$, respectively, and the centres $O$ and $O'$ of the two hemispheres both lie on the $X$ axis. The $Z'$ axis and the $Z$ axis are a distance $t=3R/10$ apart, and the length of the cylindrical part of the vessel is $l=2R$. The straight line through the pair of suspension points of the vessel intersects the $XOZ$ plane at the point $Q$, whose coordinates are $(x_Q=-R/10,\ z_Q=2\sqrt{3}R/11)$. The material of the vessel is uniform, and its density $\rho_1$ is 3 times the density $\rho_2$ of water. Friction is neglected.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2020-1-7-fig1.jpg

Figure 7a

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2020-1-7-fig2.png

Figure 7b

(1) Find the angle between the $Z$ axis and the vertical when the empty vessel hangs freely in equilibrium.

(2) Find the moment of inertia of the empty vessel about the axis through the pair of suspension points, and the angular frequency of its small oscillations about the equilibrium position (it is known that the moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere of density $\rho$ and radius $R$ about an axis through its centre of mass is $I_1=\dfrac{8}{15}\pi\rho R^{5}$, and that the moment of inertia of a uniform solid cylinder of radius $R$ and length $L$ about an axis through its centre of mass parallel to the base of the cylinder is $I_2=\dfrac{\pi\rho R^{2}L(3R^{2}+L^{2})}{12}$).

(3) The empty vessel is left to hang freely, and water is slowly poured into it. For what distance $h$ from the water surface in the vessel to its bottom does the body of the vessel stand upright?

(4) Briefly state the critical condition for the vessel to "overturn when full".

Problem 1

A small circular hole in an opaque thin sheet is shown in Fig. 1a as the part between the black segments; its radius OM is $1.00\,\mathrm{mm}$. Light from a helium–neon laser of wavelength $\lambda = 632.8\,\mathrm{nm}$ is used as the light source and is incident normally, as a parallel beam, on the hole from its left side. On the symmetry axis perpendicular to the hole, on the right side, there is a point P. Relative to the point P, the wavefront at the hole can be regarded as a combination of half-period zones: with P as centre, and with the distance from P to the centre O of the hole denoted by $r_0$ ($r_0 \gg \lambda$), draw spheres of radii $r_0+\frac{\lambda}{2}$, $r_0+2\times\frac{\lambda}{2}$, $r_0+3\times\frac{\lambda}{2}$, $\cdots$; these divide the wavefront in the plane of the hole into $N$ annular zones ($N$ a natural number), the distance from P to the edge M of the hole being $r_0+N\frac{\lambda}{2}$; the zone of smallest radius is a disc. The annular zones divided in this way are called half-period zones (because the optical path difference from corresponding edges of adjacent zones to the point P is $\frac{\lambda}{2}$). Clearly, the number $N$ of zones determines the position of the point P. When the original half-period zones need to be re-divided or merged, consider only re-dividing each existing half-period zone into several new half-period zones, or merging several existing half-period zones into one new half-period zone.

(2) Let $N = 4$ (a 4-zone zone plate), and let a transparent material be placed over the 1st and 3rd half-period zones (the grey parts in Fig. 1b), so that the light passing through this transparent material gains an optical path of $\frac{\lambda}{2}$. Find

problems.problem:
Problem 2

In June 2021 the Shenzhou-12 crewed rocket successfully docked with the Tiangong space station; this involves the problem of a chaser (the Shenzhou-12 rocket) meeting a target (the space station) in orbits around the Earth. In this problem the Hohmann transfer scheme is used to investigate how the chaser changes its velocity (speed and direction) so as to dock (meet) with a target in a fixed orbit.

As shown in Fig. 2a, the target A and the chaser c both move counterclockwise with speed $v_0$ on a circular orbit of radius $r_0$. At time 0 their positions are respectively

$$\theta_{\mathrm{A},i} = \theta_0,\quad \theta_{\mathrm{c},i} = 0,\quad r_{\mathrm{A},i} = r_{\mathrm{c},i} = r_0$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2021-1-2-fig1.png

Fig. 2a. [目标A = target A; 中心 = centre; 追击者c = chaser c]

At this moment the chaser c fires its engine instantaneously, and its velocity changes instantaneously by $\Delta\boldsymbol{v}$ (as shown in Fig. 2b); the orbit of c also changes instantaneously from the circular orbit of radius $r_0$ to the elliptical orbit shown in Fig. 2c. The angle between the major axis of the elliptical orbit and the direction of the polar axis (the line from the centre to the position of c at the moment of firing) is $\phi$ ($\phi$ is measured clockwise). The angle between the direction of motion of c and the direction of the polar axis is denoted by $\theta_\mathrm{c}$ (the positive direction of $\theta_\mathrm{c}$ is counterclockwise), and the distance of c from the centre is $r_\mathrm{c}(\theta_\mathrm{c})$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2021-1-2-fig2.png

Fig. 2b [追击者c = chaser c; 椭圆轨道 = elliptical orbit; 圆轨道 = circular orbit]

(1) Given the mass $m$, the energy $E$ (in fact the total mechanical energy of the system formed by the flying object and the Earth) and the angular momentum $L$ of the flying object, express the orbital parameters $R$ and $\varepsilon$ in terms of $E$, $L$, $m$ and the given parameters $r_0$, $v_0$, etc. It is known that a standard elliptical orbit (major axis along the polar axis) has, in polar coordinates (origin at the right focus), the form

$$r(\theta) = \frac{R}{1+\varepsilon\cos\theta}$$

where $R$ is the orbit size parameter and $\varepsilon$ is the orbital eccentricity; together they are called the orbital parameters.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2021-1-2-fig3.png

Fig. 2c [目标A = target A; 追击者c = chaser c; 中心 = centre; 第一类汇合点 = rendezvous point of the first kind; 第二类汇合点 = rendezvous point of the second kind]

(2) Write the expression for the orbit $r_\mathrm{c}(\theta_\mathrm{c})$ of the chaser c after firing (see Fig. 2c), in terms of $r_0$, the eccentricity $\varepsilon$ and $\phi$.

(3) Write the ratio $T_\mathrm{c}/T_\mathrm{A}$ of the orbital period $T_\mathrm{c}$ of the chaser c after firing to the period $T_\mathrm{A}$ of the target A, in terms of $\varepsilon$ and $\phi$.

(4) Define two firing parameters (see Fig. 2b): the dimensionless relative velocity change $\delta = \left|\frac{\Delta\boldsymbol{v}}{\boldsymbol{v}_0}\right|$, and the angle $\alpha$ between $\Delta\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\boldsymbol{v}_0$ ($\alpha = 0$ when they coincide; the clockwise direction is taken as positive). Express the eccentricity $\varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon\cos\phi$ of the orbit of the chaser c in terms of the firing parameters $\delta$ and $\alpha$.

(5) Consider the case in which the chaser c and the target A meet at the rendezvous point of the first kind (see Fig. 2c). Let the number of times the target A passes the rendezvous point of the first kind from time 0 be $n_\mathrm{A}$, and the number of times the chaser c passes the rendezvous point of the first kind (the starting moment not counted) be $n_\mathrm{c}$. At time 0, $\theta_{\mathrm{A},i} = \theta_0$, $\theta_{\mathrm{c},i} = 0$. Find $n_\mathrm{A}$ in terms of $n_\mathrm{c}$, $\theta_0$, $\varepsilon$ and $\phi$.

(6) Express $n_\mathrm{A}$ in terms of $\delta$ and $\alpha$. Keeping $\delta$ fixed, find the two simple, obvious extremum points $\alpha_0$ of the function $n_\mathrm{A}(\alpha)$ with respect to the variation of $\alpha$ (so that even if the firing angle $\alpha$ deviates somewhat from $\alpha_0$, the solution still holds approximately, which facilitates successful docking).

(7) If one of the above two values of $\alpha_0$ is taken,

(i) the value of $\delta$ has an upper limit $\delta_{\max}$ (i.e. if $\delta > \delta_{\max}$, the chaser c and the target A will not meet); find $\delta_{\max}$;

(ii) let the initial value of $\theta_\mathrm{A}$ be $\theta_0$; write the relation between $\delta$ and $\theta_0$, $n_\mathrm{A}$, $n_\mathrm{c}$; and find the value of $\delta$ when $\theta_0 = \frac{\pi}{2}$, $n_\mathrm{A} = 2$, $n_\mathrm{c} = 1$.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3

About one quarter of the matter in the universe may exist in the form of dark matter. Dark matter may be made up of a new kind of elementary particle. People have long been searching for interactions between dark-matter particles and known particles; one important class of experiments searches for interactions between dark-matter particles and atomic nuclei. Such experiments generally use some material as the target; when a dark-matter particle flies into the detector it collides with an atomic nucleus of the target material. In this process the originally almost stationary nucleus obtains part of the kinetic energy from the dark-matter particle and thus moves in the target material, producing light signals and electric signals. A dark-matter detector can detect these signals and thereby observe dark matter.

(1) The target material is chosen to be xenon isotope nuclei $^{132}\mathrm{Xe}$. Assume that the masses of the dark-matter particle X and of the $^{132}\mathrm{Xe}$ nucleus are both 132 times the proton mass $m_\mathrm{p}$, and that in the centre-of-mass frame of the particle X and the $^{132}\mathrm{Xe}$ nucleus the scattering is isotropic (the probabilities of the outgoing particle appearing in every direction are equal). A dark-matter particle X enters the detector along the $z$ direction with speed $200\,\mathrm{km/s}$ and collides with a $^{132}\mathrm{Xe}$ target nucleus at rest. Derive, in the laboratory frame (the reference frame in which the $^{132}\mathrm{Xe}$ target nucleus is at rest before the collision), after the collision,

(i) the relation between the momentum of the $^{132}\mathrm{Xe}$ nucleus and its emission angle;

(ii) the angular distribution of the $^{132}\mathrm{Xe}$ nucleus (the probability distribution with respect to its emission angle);

(iii) the distribution of the kinetic energy of the $^{132}\mathrm{Xe}$ nucleus.

(2) The scattering cross-section is commonly used to express the strength of the interaction between two particles. The scattering cross-section is similar to a certain cross-sectional area, and the cross-sectional area can be understood as the effective area for a collision to occur between the two particles. For example, the cross-sectional area for collisions between two small rigid spheres of radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ is $\pi(r_1+r_2)^2$; this is the scattering cross-section for the collision of the two small spheres. Now the detector contains $1.0\,\mathrm{t}$ of xenon atoms, and the scattering cross-section for collisions between the dark-matter particle X and the $^{132}\mathrm{Xe}$ nucleus is $1.0\times10^{-38}\,\mathrm{cm^2}$; assume that all dark-matter particles X have speed $200\,\mathrm{km/s}$, and that the density of dark matter near the Earth is $0.40\,m_\mathrm{p}/\mathrm{cm^3}$. Find how many collisions between dark-matter particles X and $^{132}\mathrm{Xe}$ nuclei occur in this detector per year. Avogadro's number is $N_\mathrm{A} = 6.023\times10^{23}$. For simplicity, take the molar mass of the proton as $1.0\,\mathrm{g/mol}$.

(3) The signal detected by the detector is produced by the kinetic energy obtained by the $^{132}\mathrm{Xe}$ nucleus in the collision. However, the signal can be recorded only when this kinetic energy exceeds the threshold of the detector. Assuming that this threshold is $10\,\mathrm{keV}$, estimate how many collisions between dark-matter particles X and $^{132}\mathrm{Xe}$ nuclei this detector can detect per year. The rest mass of the proton is $0.94\,\mathrm{GeV}/c^2$, where $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum.

(4) The speeds of dark-matter particles in the Galaxy obey a certain distribution $f(v)$, and the speed of dark-matter particles has an upper limit $v_{\max}$, i.e. $f(v) = 0$ when $v > v_{\max}$. Answer: what causes this upper limit?

(5) For a laboratory reference frame on the Earth, the upper limit of the speed distribution of dark-matter particles is $0.002$ times the speed of light in vacuum. Moreover, in fact we do not know the mass of the dark-matter particle. Below what mass of the dark-matter particle will the above detector be unable to detect dark-matter signals?

problems.title: Problem 4
problems.problem:
Problem 4

Electrical interactions play a very important role in living organisms. When a DNA-like acidic molecule is placed in water, some loosely attached atoms on the molecule may dissociate; the positive ions drift away, leaving some electrons behind, so that this macromolecule becomes negatively charged. Similarly, cell membranes in water can also become negatively charged for this reason, and the electrostatic repulsion between them can keep these macromolecules or cell membranes from "clumping together". Since matter itself is electrically neutral, the solution contains a large number of drifting positive ions, which causes the electrostatic force between these macromolecules to decay with distance. At room temperature $T$, consider the following questions:

(1) (i) Consider the region near the outer side of a negatively charged cell membrane (facing the region where the positive ions drift), close to its surface. Here the cell membrane can be regarded as an infinitely large plane. Take the $x$ axis perpendicular to the outer surface of the cell membrane, pointing towards the outside of the membrane, with the origin on the outer surface of the membrane. The dielectric constant (permittivity) of the solution surrounding the membrane is $\varepsilon$, and the surface charge density uniformly distributed on the outer surface of the membrane is $-\sigma$ ($\sigma > 0$). The system and its surroundings are in thermal equilibrium. Owing to the electrostatic interaction, the density of positive ions in the solution is not uniform, but each local part can be regarded as being in equilibrium. Here the behaviour of the positive ions is similar to that of atmospheric molecules above the ground, except that here the positive ions are acted on by the electrostatic field, while atmospheric molecules are acted on by the gravitational field. Take the number density of positive ions at the outer surface of the membrane, $n_0$, as a constant to be determined. Write the differential equation satisfied by the electric potential $\varphi$ near the outer surface of the membrane. The charge of the electron is $-e$, the charge of a positive ion is $+e$, and the Boltzmann constant is $k$; neglect gravity and the buoyancy of water. Hint: according to Boltzmann statistics, the probability for a particle to be in a state of energy $E$ is proportional to $\exp\left(-\frac{E}{kT}\right)$, where $T$ is the absolute temperature of the equilibrium state of the particle.

(ii) The liquid tissue inside the surface of the cell membrane can be regarded as a conductor; take the potential on the membrane surface to be zero. Write the boundary conditions satisfied by the potential $\varphi$ on the outer surface of the membrane.

(iii) Under the given boundary conditions, take the logarithmic function $\varphi(x) = A\ln(1+Bx)$ as a trial solution of the differential equation obtained in (1)(i). Find the values of the constants $n_0$, $A$, $B$, and express $\varphi(x)$ and $n(x)$ (the number density of positive ions at $x$) in terms of $\sigma$, $\varepsilon$, $T$, $e$, $k$;

(iv) Verify that the $n(x)$ obtained guarantees the electrical neutrality of the whole system.

(v) Find the electrostatic field energy $U_\mathrm{f}$ in a sufficiently tall cylindrical volume whose base is a unit area of the charged outer surface of the membrane, and the total electrostatic potential energy $U_\mathrm{e}$ of all the positive ions in the same volume.

(2) Consider the case in which two cells are close to each other. The outer sides of the two cell membranes and this system between them can be studied with the following simplified model: two uniformly negatively charged infinitely large parallel plates, each with surface charge density $-\sigma$, separated by a distance $2D$. The point midway between the two plates is taken as the origin of coordinates, the $x$ axis is perpendicular to the plates, the potential at the origin is taken as zero, and the number density of positive ions at the origin, $n_0$, is a parameter to be determined. Take the function $\varphi(x) = A\ln[\cos(Bx)]$ as a trial solution of the differential equation.

(i) From the differential equation satisfied by $\varphi(x)$, determine the constants $A$, $B$, expressed in terms of $T$, $\varepsilon$, $e$, $k$, $n_0$.

(ii) Find $n_0$, expressed in terms of $D$, $\sigma$, $\varepsilon$, $T$, $e$, $k$, $\theta$ (if a transcendental equation is encountered, it need not be solved; denote the solution of that equation in the physical region by $\theta$).

(iii) Give the difference $\Delta n \equiv n(\pm D) - n_0$ between the number densities of positive ions at the outer surfaces of the cells and at the centre between the two membranes, expressed in terms of $\sigma$, $\varepsilon$, $T$, $k$.

(iv) Verify that the $n(x)$ obtained guarantees the electrical neutrality of the whole system.

(v) Give the resultant force per unit area acting on a charged plane (cell membrane). It is known that the inside and outside of the cell membranes are both filled with water of the same density. Hint: positive ions in water behave similarly to an ideal gas, and are locally in thermal equilibrium.

(vi) With other conditions unchanged, and on the premise that the two plates can still be regarded as infinitely large, discuss how the magnitude of the resultant force per unit area on a charged plane varies with the distance $D$ in the two different limiting cases of short distance and long distance.

problems.title: Problem 5
problems.problem:
Problem 5

(1) The spin magnetic moment of an electron is

$$\boldsymbol{\mu} = \frac{-e}{m}\boldsymbol{S}$$

where $-e$ ($e > 0$) is the charge of the electron, $m$ is the electron mass, $\frac{-e}{m}$ is the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron; $\boldsymbol{S}$ is the spin angular momentum, whose $z$ component $S_z$ can take only two values: $S_z = \frac{1}{2}\hbar$ for spin up and $S_z = -\frac{1}{2}\hbar$ for spin down, where $\hbar = \frac{h}{2\pi}$ and $h$ is the Planck constant. Assume that the magnetic moment of a molecule or atom equals the spin magnetic moment of one electron.

(i) When a paramagnet is placed in an external magnetic field, it becomes magnetized because the probabilities of its molecular magnetic moments being aligned parallel or antiparallel to the field direction change; the degree of magnetization is described by the magnetic moment per unit volume (the magnetization) $\boldsymbol{M}$, $\boldsymbol{M} = \chi\boldsymbol{H}$, where $\chi$ is the magnetic susceptibility, $\boldsymbol{H} \equiv \frac{\boldsymbol{B}}{\mu_0} - \boldsymbol{M}$ is the magnetic field strength, $\boldsymbol{B}$ is the magnetic induction, and $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability. At ordinary temperature $T$ (absolute temperature), $\chi \ll 1$ and $kT \gg \frac{e\hbar}{2m}B$ ($k$ is the Boltzmann constant). Let the magnetic induction $\boldsymbol{B}$ be uniform and the molecular number density of the paramagnet be $n$. Using Boltzmann statistics, derive that the susceptibility of the paramagnet satisfies $\chi = \frac{C}{T}$, and give the expression for $C$. It is known that, according to Boltzmann statistics, the probability for a particle to be in an energy state is proportional to $\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{E}{kT}}$, where $E$ is the energy of that state and $T$ is the absolute temperature of the equilibrium state of the particle.

(ii) A ferromagnet differs from a paramagnet: below the Curie temperature, a ferromagnet can produce a rather strong magnetism in an environment without an external magnetic field; this is called spontaneous magnetization. Spontaneous magnetization occurs in "magnetic domains"; in each "magnetic domain" the molecular magnetic moments are all aligned along the same direction (parallel alignment), and the ferromagnet is then in the ferromagnetic phase. The reason for the parallel alignment of the magnetic moments is a quantum effect; it can also be regarded as there being a very strong equivalent magnetic field inside, which Weiss called the "molecular field". The "molecular field" is about 3 orders of magnitude larger than the magnetic field produced by one spin magnetic moment at the interatomic distance. Above the Curie temperature the ferromagnet turns into a paramagnet, and its susceptibility obeys the Curie–Weiss law $\chi = \frac{C}{T-\theta}$ (where $\theta$ is the Curie temperature); this differs from an ordinary paramagnet, and the difference comes from the "molecular field" $H_m$ inside the ferromagnet, which can be expressed as $H_m = \gamma M$. Assume that the molecular number density of the ferromagnet is also $n$. Give the expression for $\gamma$ (the Curie temperature $\theta$ may be regarded as known); and derive the expression for the molecular field $H_m$ in the case in which all the magnetic moments are aligned parallel.

(2) In a ferromagnetic crystal the atoms are arranged on periodic lattice sites. The magnetic field felt by each atom can be understood as the average value of the "molecular field" provided by the atoms on its nearest-neighbour lattice sites.

(i) Consider the one-dimensional lattice spin system shown in Fig. 5a, in which the magnetic moments on all lattice sites are aligned parallel. The Curie temperature of this system is $\theta$. Assume that the relation between $H_m$ and $\theta$ derived in the previous question still holds, and that this system contains $N$ ($N \gg 1$) lattice sites, with one atom on each site; when spontaneous magnetization occurs, the spins of the atoms are aligned parallel, and this alignment makes the energy of the system lowest. Give the equivalent magnetic field produced at this time by one spin at its nearest-neighbour lattice site, and the magnetic energy of the whole system.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2021-1-5-fig1.png

Fig. 5a

(ii) Suppose that the spin on some non-end lattice site of this one-dimensional lattice spin system flips and becomes antiparallel, as shown in Fig. 5b. Compared with the situation of Fig. 5a, by how much has the energy of the system increased?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2021-1-5-fig2.png

Fig. 5b

(3) If the atomic spins are alternately aligned in opposite directions, the material is called an antiferromagnet. An antiferromagnet has a special lattice structure: the structure consists of an A-site lattice and a B-site lattice, as shown in Fig. 5c. The nearest neighbours of an A site are B, and the next-nearest neighbours are A; similarly for the B sites. The nearest-neighbour "molecular field" of an antiferromagnet is opposite in direction to that of a ferromagnet, and besides the nearest-neighbour spins, the next-nearest-neighbour spins also contribute to the "molecular field". The "molecular fields" at the A and B sites can then be expressed respectively as

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2021-1-5-fig3.png

Fig. 5c

$$\boldsymbol{H}_{\mathrm{mA}} = -\alpha_{\mathrm{AB}}\boldsymbol{\mu}_\mathrm{B} - \alpha_{\mathrm{AA}}\boldsymbol{\mu}_\mathrm{A},\quad \boldsymbol{H}_{\mathrm{mB}} = -\alpha_{\mathrm{AB}}\boldsymbol{\mu}_\mathrm{A} - \alpha_{\mathrm{BB}}\boldsymbol{\mu}_\mathrm{B},$$

where $\boldsymbol{\mu}_\mathrm{A}$, $\boldsymbol{\mu}_\mathrm{B}$ are the spin magnetic moments on the A and B sites respectively. Assume that all atoms on A sites are identical and all atoms on B sites are identical; then $\alpha_{\mathrm{AA}} = \alpha_{\mathrm{BB}} = \alpha$, $\alpha_{\mathrm{AB}} = \alpha_{\mathrm{BA}} = \beta$, $\beta > |\alpha|$.

(i) Give the magnetic energy of an antiferromagnet with $N$ lattice sites ($N/2$ sites each of A and B);

(ii) The Néel temperature is the temperature above which the antiferromagnetic phase disappears and the antiferromagnet becomes paramagnetic. At this time the magnetizations and magnetic fields of the A-site lattice and the B-site lattice satisfy respectively

$$M_\mathrm{A} = \frac{C}{2T}H_\mathrm{A},\quad M_\mathrm{B} = \frac{C}{2T}H_\mathrm{B},$$

where the coefficient $C$ is the same as in question (1)(i). Give the Néel temperature of the one-dimensional antiferromagnet.

(4) Now consider another situation: the atoms are distributed on a square lattice with lattice constant $a$ in the two-dimensional $x$-$y$ plane, and the magnetic moments of the atoms can rotate within the plane. As shown in Fig. 5d, within a planar region of size $L$ ($L \gg a$), the magnetic moments are distributed as indicated by the arrows on the lattice sites. Owing to the "molecular field" effect, there is a rather strong interaction between magnetic moments, and this interaction is significant only between nearest-neighbour molecules. Let the angle between the spin angular momentum $\boldsymbol{S}_i$ on the $i$-th lattice site in this plane and the $x$ axis be $\theta_i \in [0, 2\pi]$; the magnetic energy of the system can be expressed as

$$E(\{\theta_i\}) = -J'\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\boldsymbol{S}_i\cdot\boldsymbol{S}_j = -J\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\cos(\theta_i-\theta_j)$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2021-1-5-fig4.png

Fig. 5d

where $J'$, $J$ ($J', J > 0$) are constants, $\langle i,j\rangle$ denotes all nearest-neighbour pairs of lattice sites $i$ and $j$ (a lattice site generally has four nearest-neighbour lattice sites), and the configuration of the system is given by $\{\theta_i\}$. Assume that the system has reached thermal equilibrium with its surroundings and that the volume of the system is unchanged; the Helmholtz free energy is then $F = E - TS$, where $E$ is the internal energy of the system and $S$ is the entropy of the system.

(i) A vortex configuration that may exist in the system is shown in Fig. 5e. Going once around a closed loop surrounding the vortex centre, the sum of the differences of the orientation angles of the magnetic moments of nearest-neighbour lattice sites $\langle i,j\rangle$ on this closed loop is

$$\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}(\theta_i-\theta_j) = 2\pi l$$

Here $l$ is a positive integer related to the vortex structure; the case $l = 1$ is shown in Fig. 5e. For convenience, consider a closed loop (circle) centred on the vortex centre with a rather large radius $r$; find the average value $\langle\theta_i-\theta_j\rangle$ of the differences of the orientation angles of adjacent lattice sites on the circle.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2021-1-5-fig5.png

Fig. 5e

(ii) When the radius $r$ of the loop around the vortex centre is rather large, it can be approximately assumed that the magnetic moments are arranged successively on a series of concentric circles whose radii differ by $a$, and that the angle between nearest-neighbour magnetic moments on adjacent concentric circles can be taken as zero. The same approximation is made for the region of small radius, which has little effect on the total energy. From this, estimate the energy of the vortex system shown in Fig. 5e.

(iii) If the centre of the vortex is placed at different positions, the system can be regarded as being in different states. Assuming that there is only one vortex on a square lattice of size $L$ and lattice constant $a$, estimate the possible number of states $\Omega$, and then calculate the entropy of the system $S \equiv k\ln\Omega$.

(iv) If there exists some temperature above and below which the properties of the system differ markedly, a phase transition may have occurred. For a vortex system, find the possible phase-transition temperature and explain.

problems.title: Problem 5
problems.problem:
Problem 5

Laser cooling of atoms is a technique that uses laser light to slow atoms down and lower the atomic temperature. The Zeeman slower used in cold-atom experiments to decelerate an atomic beam is shown in Figure 5a: a beam of single-frequency laser light propagating opposite to the collimated atomic beam scatters off the atoms, so as to decelerate them. The scattering process between atoms and photons can be understood as the atom absorbing a photon and then isotropically emitting a photon of the same energy. The number of photons scattered by one atom per unit time is called the scattering rate. When the atomic energy levels are in resonance with the laser frequency, the scattering rate of photons by the atom is largest and the deceleration is most effective. However, under normal circumstances, once the atomic velocity changes (the atom is slowed down), because of the Doppler effect the atom is no longer in resonance with the laser, and the deceleration stops. The Zeeman slower makes use of the property that atomic transition frequencies are affected by a magnetic field (the Zeeman effect: the atomic energy levels are affected by an external magnetic field, so that the frequency of light absorbed in transitions between levels is also affected by the external magnetic field), and uses a spatially varying magnetic field to compensate for the Doppler effect, so that the atoms are in resonance with the laser everywhere in the slowing tube, until the atoms are decelerated almost to rest.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cpho-2021-2-5-fig1.png

Figure 5a

[Labels in the figure: 原子炉 = atomic oven; 准直管 = collimation tube; 减速管 = slowing tube; 线圈（提供非均匀磁场） = coils (providing a non-uniform magnetic field); 冷原子实验腔 = cold-atom experimental chamber; 减速激光 = slowing laser.]

(1) Consider a gas of $^{40}\mathrm{K}$ atoms heated to $350\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. What is the root-mean-square speed $v_0$ of the atoms after collimation (assume that after collimation the atoms have only one translational degree of freedom)?

(2) When the laser is in resonance with the corresponding atomic transition, the scattering rate of photons by the atom is $\Gamma = 5.00\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The wavelength of the laser used to decelerate the atoms is known to be $670\,\mathrm{nm}$. What is the acceleration $a$ of the atom during its decelerated motion? What is the distance needed to decelerate to rest a $^{40}\mathrm{K}$ atom with the root-mean-square speed $v_0$, if it is kept in resonance with the laser all the time?

(3) Ignoring the influence of the magnetic field, calculate by how much the laser frequency should be lowered below the laser resonance frequency of the atom at rest in order to produce a resonant transition with an atom moving (towards the light source) at the root-mean-square speed $v_0$.

(4) It is known that, under the action of a magnetic field, the frequency of the corresponding atomic transition decreases linearly as the magnetic induction increases (the Zeeman effect):

$$f_0(B) = f_0(B=0) + \beta B$$

where the coefficient $\beta = -1.00\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{Hz/T}$. Assume that at the exit of the collimation tube ($z = 0$) the $^{40}\mathrm{K}$ atoms move towards the direction from which the laser comes with the root-mean-square speed $v_0$, and assume also that the magnetic induction $B$ at the exit of the collimation tube ($z = 0$) is 0.
